name: A LEAGUE OF PEAR OWN BURGER

recipe.history:
The pear is one of humanity's oldest cultivated fruits, with origins tracing back over four thousand years to the temperate regions of western China and Central Asia. Ancient Romans adored the pear so deeply that the agricultural writer Pliny the Elder catalogued over forty distinct varieties in the first century AD. From Rome, pear cultivation spread westward through Europe, finding particular devotion in France, where the Bartlett pear — known there as Williams — was developed in the eighteenth century and became the gold standard of the variety. The Bartlett's buttery, sweet flesh and floral aroma made it the ideal candidate for cooking, preserving, and eating fresh, and French pâtissiers and confectioners elevated it into jams, tarts, and compotes of extraordinary refinement. The pear carries with it a cultural weight — it is the fruit of patience, of autumn, of the slow satisfaction that comes from waiting for something to ripen fully.

The pear arrived in America in the early colonial period, carried by European settlers who planted orchards up and down the Eastern Seaboard. It took hold in the Pacific Northwest with particular vigor, and by the nineteenth century, Oregon and Washington had become the pear capitals of the New World. American cooks, never shy about sweetness, discovered that roasted pear offered something uniquely compelling alongside savory preparations — the caramelized sugars playing off salt and fat in ways that apple and other fruits could not quite replicate. The burger world was slow to embrace fruit toppings, but adventurous chefs in the American craft burger renaissance of the 1990s and 2000s began experimenting with roasted and poached pears atop beef patties, discovering that the fruit's floral sweetness cut through the richness of the meat with elegant precision. Pear jam, too, found its way onto the bun as a counterpoint to sharp cheeses and peppery greens.

I remember the first time I roasted a Bartlett pear for a burger. It was late September, the kind of afternoon where the light comes in low and golden through the kitchen window, and I had a surplus of slightly overripe pears from the farmers market that I simply could not let go to waste. I halved them, drizzled them with a little honey and a pinch of cardamom, and slid them into a hot oven while I shaped my patties. When I pulled the pears out — edges caramelized, flesh yielding and fragrant — I layered them onto a freshly griddled beef patty alongside a smear of homemade pear jam, some sharp aged Gruyère, and a handful of bitter arugula. The first bite stopped me cold. It was a burger that tasted like autumn itself, like something that had been waiting to be invented for a very long time. I ate it standing at the counter, not wanting to interrupt the experience by sitting down.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — to that internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is not a preference but a philosophy, a statement about respect for the ingredient and the diner. At medium rare, the beef retains its natural moisture, its fat has begun to render and baste the meat from within, and the Maillard crust on the exterior creates a textural and flavor contrast that is nothing short of architectural. To cook beyond this point is to chase the juices out, to transform a living, complex thing into something dry and monotone. The pear topping on this burger thrives in the presence of a medium rare patty precisely because both share a quality of yielding softness meeting caramelized depth — the roasted pear's edges echo the sear on the beef, and the jammy interior of the pear mirrors the rosy, tender center of the patty. Medium rare is the only temperature that honors the full intention of this burger.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
2 ripe Bartlett pears, halved and cored
2 Bartlett pears, peeled, cored, and diced
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: Dissolve yeast in warm milk with 1 tsp of the sugar and let sit 5–10 minutes until foamy. Combine flour, remaining sugar, and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook.

2. Add the yeast mixture and 3 eggs to the flour. Mix on medium speed until a shaggy dough forms, about 3 minutes. Add butter one tablespoon at a time, allowing each addition to incorporate before adding the next. Mix on medium-high for 8 minutes until dough is smooth, glossy, and pulls away from the bowl.
3. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (or at least 8 hours) for a slow, flavor-developing rise.

4. Divide chilled dough into 6 equal pieces (about 90g each). Shape into tight rounds by pulling the surface tension downward. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover loosely, and proof at room temperature 2–3 hours until doubled and puffy.

5. Preheat oven to 375°F. Beat remaining egg with 1 tbsp water and brush tops of buns gently. Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool completely on a wire rack.

6. Make the pear jam: Combine diced pears, sugar, lemon juice, vanilla, and ground ginger in a small saucepan over medium heat. Cook, stirring frequently, until pears break down and mixture thickens to a jam consistency, 20–25 minutes. Use a potato masher or fork to break up large chunks. Let cool to room temperature; refrigerate until needed.

7. Roast the Bartlett pears: Preheat oven to 400°F. Place pear halves cut-side up on a baking sheet. Brush with melted butter, drizzle with honey, dust with cardamom, and add a pinch of salt. Roast 20–25 minutes until caramelized and tender. Let cool slightly, then slice each half into 3–4 wedges.

8. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 6 portions (about 4 oz each). Gently form into patties about 3/4 inch thick, pressing a shallow dimple in the center of each to prevent bulging during cooking. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Refrigerate patties 15 minutes before cooking.

9. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat until just beginning to smoke. Add neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place patties dimple-side up and cook undisturbed 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once, place a slice of Gruyère on each patty, and cook 2–3 more minutes until internal temperature reaches 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Tent loosely with foil and rest 3–4 minutes.
10. Dress the arugula: Toss baby arugula with olive oil, fresh lemon juice, and a pinch of flaky salt just before assembling.
11. Toast the buns: Split buns and toast cut-side down on the griddle or in a dry skillet over medium heat for 1–2 minutes until golden.

12. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of pear jam on the bottom bun. Place the rested, cheese-topped patty on top. Fan 3–4 roasted pear wedges over the cheese. Pile dressed arugula on top. Crown with the top bun and serve immediately.
